Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette:
Farid is a 78-year-old Middle Eastern American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a roofer, a trade he continued into older age in a reduced but still regular way because he took pride in staying useful. He is married and lives with his wife, and when he first described the event that had stayed with him, he did so haltingly. He said that when he tries to bring it up on purpose, the memory does not come in an orderly sequence. He loses parts of it, cannot hold onto the details he is looking for, and becomes frustrated by how inaccessible it feels. Yet at other times it arrives without invitation, cutting into ordinary moments with a force that feels immediate and bodily.

The trauma occurred during a job involving toxic chemical exposure. Farid had been working on a roof where industrial materials were being used nearby, and what remains most vivid in his account is not a clean narrative but the sense of danger and contamination around him as the exposure unfolded. The event has never settled into something finished in his mind. Instead, he is often overtaken by it in fragments or in sudden waves of feeling that seem to belong to that moment even when no full picture appears. He described times when he is not consciously remembering anything specific, but his body is seized by the same fear and alarm, as if the event is happening again somewhere just outside language. That loss of control over when the memory comes makes him feel exposed in his own daily life.

In the months and years afterward, Farid noticed that certain situations began to affect him sharply. News stories related to chemical incidents or public safety reports catch him off guard. If the television is on and a segment mentions a toxic spill, hazardous exposure, or an investigation into dangerous materials, he feels himself tense before he can think. His wife has seen him go still in his chair, eyes fixed but distant, as though something has grabbed him internally. He also reacts strongly to being around children. What unsettles him is not children in the abstract but the immediate sense of vulnerability their presence brings up for him. When he sees children playing near work sites, on sidewalks, or even gathered outside a school while he is driving to a roofing job, he becomes acutely distressed. The event is tied in his mind to the possibility of innocent people being harmed, and children now feel like a painful reminder of danger that can arrive without warning. Related people are difficult as well. Running into someone connected to the incident, or even hearing their name, can pull him abruptly into the same emotional state, leaving him shaken for hours.

These reactions have become woven into his work life. On roofing jobs, he is already physically alert from years of balancing at heights, but now his vigilance extends far beyond the demands of the task. If a coworker comes up behind him and puts a hand on his shoulder without warning, Farid startles with obvious alarm. He may jerk away, spin around, or snap out a sharp response before he recognizes where he is. He feels embarrassed afterward, especially with younger workers, but says his body reacts before his mind catches up. Even in places he knows are safe-at home after dinner, sitting beside his wife, or resting at the end of the day-he cannot relax. He remains keyed up, as if he must stay ready. Night brings little relief. He has trouble falling asleep, and when he does sleep it is often broken, leaving him tired and irritable the next day.

Over time, these patterns have narrowed his world. He avoids conversations when he suspects someone may bring up the exposure or similar incidents in the news. He is careful around neighbors and acquaintances connected in any way to what happened, preferring to leave quickly rather than risk being drawn into discussion. His wife has noticed that he is more withdrawn at family gatherings, particularly when grandchildren are present. He does not explain much in the moment; he simply becomes tense, quiet, and eager to step outside or go home.

What finally brought Farid to seek help was the sense that these experiences were not easing with time and that he was becoming a different kind of husband and grandfather than he wanted to be. He was particularly shaken after a recent news report and a separate moment at work when unexpected touch from a coworker made him react so strongly that everyone stopped and stared. He said he is tired of feeling ambushed by his own mind and body. What frightens him most is that the memory can remain unreachable when he tries to speak about it, then take hold of him when he least expects it. What he hopes for now is not to erase what happened, but to be able to sit with his family, be around children, and move through a workday without feeling that danger is suddenly back in the room.
